title: Core self-evaluation: self-esteem, self-monitoring and locus of control
summary: How people see themselves: self-esteem, self-monitoring, and locus of control with its effect on performance.

chunks.heading: Core self-evaluation
chunks.explanation_md:
**Core self-evaluation** is the self-perspective: how much people like or dislike themselves.

**Positive** core self-evaluation: people see themselves as capable and effective, and in control of their environment.

**Negative** core self-evaluation: people tend to dislike themselves, question their capabilities and see themselves as powerless over their environment.

It has two main elements: **self-esteem** and **locus of control** (internal or external).

key_terms.meaning: The degree to which people like or dislike themselves; two main elements are self-esteem and locus of control.

chunks.exam_line: Core self-evaluation has two elements: self-esteem and locus of control. Positive: capable, in control. Negative: dislike themselves, powerless.

chunks.heading: Self-esteem and self-monitoring
chunks.explanation_md:
**Self-esteem** is the degree to which you like or dislike yourself and how worthy or unworthy you think you are. **High self-esteem** people are confident. **Low self-esteem** people seek the approval of others and require training.

**Self-monitoring** is the ability to adjust your behavior to external, situational factors.
- **Low self-monitors** show their true dispositions and attitudes in every situation, so there is consistency between who they are and what they do.
- **High self-monitors** are highly sensitive to external cues and can behave differently in different situations. They pay close attention to others' behavior, receive better performance ratings, emerge as good leaders, are more mobile in their careers and occupy central positions in organizations.

chunks.heading: Locus of control
chunks.explanation_md:
**Locus of control** is the degree to which people believe they are masters of their own destiny.

- **Internals** believe they control what happens to them.
- **Externals** believe what happens to them is controlled by outside forces such as **luck or chance**.

So an internal says "my results depend on what I do"; an external says "it is luck or outside forces".

chunks.heading: Locus of control and performance
chunks.explanation_md:
The exercise slide leads to a table titled **Locus of control and performance**. It compares conditions of work and who performs better:

- **Information processing**: when work needs complex information processing and learning, **internals perform better**. When work is simple and easy to learn, internals perform no better than externals.
- **Initiative**: when work needs initiative and independent action, **internals perform better**. When work needs compliance and conformity, **externals perform better**.
- **Motivation**: when work needs high motivation and gives valued rewards for greater effort (incentive pay for greater productivity), **internals perform better**. When work does not need great effort and rewards are not linked to it (hourly pay set by collective bargaining), **externals perform at least as well as internals**.

Use this table for a manager whose behavior changes with the belief that he can influence outcomes. When he believes outcomes depend on him (internal), he takes initiative and puts in effort. When he believes outside forces decide (external), he is better suited to work that is about compliance and conformity.
chunks.exam_line: Internals perform better in complex work, work needing initiative and highly motivating, rewarded work. Externals perform better when work needs compliance and conformity.

questions.model_answer_md:

questions.stem: Explain locus of control and how it affects performance under different work conditions.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Locus of control** is the degree to which people believe they are masters of their own destiny. **Internals** believe they control what happens to them; **externals** believe outside forces such as luck or chance do.

The deck's table links it to performance:
- **Information processing**: with complex work and learning, internals perform better; with simple, easy-to-learn work, internals perform no better than externals.
- **Initiative**: where work needs initiative and independent action, internals perform better; where it needs compliance and conformity, externals perform better.
- **Motivation**: where work needs high motivation and gives valued rewards for greater effort, such as incentive pay, internals perform better; where little effort is needed and rewards are not linked, such as hourly pay by collective bargaining, externals perform at least as well.

For managers, this means matching people to jobs: internals for complex, initiative-based, incentive-driven roles and externals for routine, rule-following roles.

Conclusion: locus of control is a key part of core self-evaluation and shapes how people perform.

questions.stem: A manager sometimes strongly believes he can influence outcomes and takes responsibility for his decisions, but at other times doubts himself and blames circumstances beyond his control. Analyse the personality-related factors behind this and explain how they account for his varying responses.
questions.model_answer_md:
The behavior points to **locus of control** and **self-esteem**, parts of core self-evaluation.

**Locus of control**: when he believes he can influence outcomes he acts as an **internal**, believing he controls what happens to him, so he takes initiative and responsibility. When he blames circumstances beyond his control he acts as an **external**, believing outside forces such as luck or chance decide results.

**Self-esteem**: when he feels worthy and capable he is confident and in control (positive core self-evaluation). When he doubts his capabilities he shows the negative pattern: questioning capabilities and feeling powerless over the environment, and may seek approval from others.

**Self-monitoring and situation**: personality is generally stable but changes in different situations, so his sensitivity to external cues can make behavior differ across situations.

**Why responses differ**: his belief about control shifts with the situation. In complex or initiative-based work, internal beliefs help performance; where he feels powerless, he complies or blames circumstances.

**Measures**: place him in work that needs initiative where he feels in control, and provide training and support where his confidence is low.

Conclusion: his varying behavior comes from shifting locus of control and self-esteem across situations.
